front.title: IPv6 has issues with 802.11 multicast reliability

abstract.t: For the IPv6 protocol stack, while IEEE 802.11 wireless networks can on a first abstraction be considered functionally identical to wired IEEE 802 networks, there are issues regarding reliability and survivability of multicast traffic. The existence of these issues has been known for some time. This document is to state that they are still being experienced, and summarize some previous and new approaches.

Additionally, this document serves to collect consensus in the IETF process to make both the IEEE and Wifi Alliance aware of these issues and request they be included in consideration for future development. 802.11 Directed Multicast Service and Flexible Multicast Service are noted as existing protocol features that may warrant more consideration. However, other solutions may be more appropriate and are left to the expertise of the IEEE and Wifi Alliance.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The following terms reference definitions or items in IEEE 802.11. Please note any context beyond the acronym expansion is given purely to aid understanding, may contain errors and truncations, and is no replacement for sufficient knowledge of the IEEE 802.11 standards.

dl.dd: Access Point. A single physical device may provide multiple instances of this function even on a single radio interfaces.

Basic Service Set. The definition of this term is relatively complex due to e.g. 802.11 mesh functionality. In the context of this document, which involves an AP, the set of stations and AP that are "joined" in 802.11 with each other.
non-access-point (non-AP) station (STA). IEEE 802.11 does not use "client" as a term, it is used here due to ease of understanding in IETF context and being colloquially common.
Distribution System. The interconnect between multiple BSS forming a single ESS. May exist within a physical device (between multiple AP functions) or between devices. Generally, IEEE 802.3 Ethernet.

Delivery Traffic Indication Map Period. An integer value, multiplied with the beacon interval to arrive at the DTIM interval. Multicast traffic, in the absence of other factors, is delivered once per DTIM interval. Signaled by the AP in beacons for a BSS.
Extended Service Set. One or more BSS that appears functionally as the same BSS to any client connected with any of them.
medium access control (MAC) protocol data unit (PDU). IEEE 802.11 specific, "down layer" data unit. Also called MAC frame in 802.11. An aggregated variant (A-MPDU) exists.

medium access control (MAC) service data unit (SDU). More generic, "up layer" data unit that may be carried over a DS between APs, and may take the form of an Ethernet frame in that case. An aggregated variant (A-MSDU) exists in 802.11 context.

basic service set (BSS) transition; a client switching its association from one BSS to another BSS within the same ESS. The term "roaming" is present in IEEE 802.11 but not as an exclusive, unambiguous reference to specifically this kind of transition.

section.t: Additionally, the following terms are used:

dl.dd: Data unit of the layer ("2", MAC) carrying IP and likely containing additional outer headers/encapsulation of an IP header.

Participant in IP on a broadcast domain, using a single interface with a single lower-layer address. In IPv6, will almost always have multiple IPv6 addresses even in the same cope. An IP router consists of multiple hosts for the purposes of this document.
Data unit of IP ("layer 3") without further outer headers or encapsulation.

section.name: Fundamental IPv6 reliability
section.t: For IPv6 to function correctly, hosts must receive traffic addressed to a set of multicast addresses. Specifically, router advertisements sent to ff02::1 (33:33:00:00:00:01) and address resolution traffic addressed to target-address-specific groups (cf. ). Losing some or all of this traffic makes IPv6 unreliable or entirely nonfunctional.

Receiving multicast traffic is power intensive for 802.11 clients since they need to wake up their receivers quite frequently even if there is no network activity. In the normal case, multicast traffic is sent after beacons, in 100ms intervals (the DTIM period AP-side setting can affect this.)

In response, a number of 802.11 implementations have started to simply skip a chosen subset of these events, likely in violation of the 802.11 standard. As IPv4 is less reliant on broadcast/multicast, this frequently does not break IPv4. IPv6 connectivity, however, is adversely affected by the resulting loss of some multicast traffic.
Albeit somewhat difficult to gather data for, there is a sufficient amount of input being heard at the IETF that IPv6 is in fact suffering from issues due to multicast reliability.

section.name: mDNS (and other multicast) roaming issues
section.t: A related but distinct issue in the reliability of IPv6 multicast exists in delivery of mDNS multicast traffic after an 802.11 client device roams to another 802.11 access point. mDNS uses the IPv6 multicast group ff02::fb and the IPv6 host will report that group as joined using MLD.

If the access point or another device in the network (802.11 DS) between access points performs MLD snooping, these devices will be maintaining a table for each multicast group, tracking joins based on either IPv6 addresses, MAC addresses or ports.

If additionally the IPv6 end host stack is unaware of 802.11 roaming events, or hasn't connected them into the MLD implementation, it will not re-report the group as joined by sending MLD until either queried again or the mDNS component leaves and rejoins the group. A MLD querier is necessary for MLD snooping operation, therefore this typically results in a period of a few seconds to minutes (depending on the querier's timer configuration) where MLD snooping state does not reflect the joined group. mDNS then receives no advertisements, service discovery does not work and a poor user experience results.

There is also an unfortunate crosslinking of this issue with attempted fixes to general IPv6 reliability: multicast to unicast conversion requires the AP to be aware of which clients are joined to a given group. The means for the AP to acquire this data is MLD snooping. Attempts to fix general IPv6 reliability by further use of multicast to unicast conversion may thus have worsened mDNS issues.

The considerations in this section also apply to other protocols using multicast, but were primarily reported regarding mDNS. There is currently no standardized protocol to transfer MLD state between devices performing MLD snooping.

section.name: Increasing DTIM period
section.t: The DTIM period is generally an operator accessible setting on their 802.11 installation, though not all devices (particularly intended for home use) may expose it. Raising the DTIM period, e.g. to 5, is reported to alleviate the general IPv6 reliability issues, since client devices seem to consider this as sufficiently power efficient and not perform further aggressive multicast dropping.

Values larger than 5 SHOULD NOT be used as they may interfere with IPv4 Proxy ARP functions, some of which use a 600ms delay by default. If this is known to not apply to a given product or installation, higher values MAY be usable. However, larger values also result in higher latency on multicast delivery, which will be visible to end users as e.g. delay on mDNS discovery.

section.name: Increasing IPv6 RA frequency
section.t: Since the power save behavior at issue results in a roughly random drop of some percentage of multicast traffic (i.e. assuming it does not synchronize with a device's regular extra drop periods), it is possible to achieve a higher delivery chance for IPv6 router advertisements by sending them more frequently or in bursts. This is also normally available to the operator to tune, though again not necessarily on devices intended for home use.
This approach, if seen at large, is likely to result in a "race to the bottom" where networks send more and more traffic, and devices drop more and more traffic.

If this approach is intentionally added to an RA sender implementation, it MUST ensure there is sufficient variance in RA transmission timers at the sub-second level to avoid synchronizing with an 802.11 client implementing aggressive power-save by sleeping through a given fraction of DTIM periods.

Beyond configuration or implementation on a router, an AP might theoretically also implement this by buffering received RAs and retransmitting them multiple times only onto its BSS side. This is anticipated to be very error prone since there may be multiple routers, each sending multiple RAs, choosing arbitrarily to distribute RA contents across them. Additionally, other than lifetimes there is no notification of specific RA contents being removed.

section.name: Flexible Multicast Service
section.t: The 802.11 Flexible Multicast Service protocol feature, introduced in 802.11v-2011, allows clients to explicitly request that some given multicast groups are buffered and delivered at less frequent intervals. The result is the same power savings as above, but since it is negotiated with the AP, the traffic loss is avoided.
Unfortunately, FMS is not mandatory to implement for 802.11 compliance and not required for Wifi Alliance certification. This document is to express IETF interest to push for FMS implementations.

section.name: Converting Multicast IPv6 Router Advertisements to Ethernet Unicast
section.t: Receiving IPv6 Router Advertisements are crucial for IPv6 hosts operation. For clients which lack FMS or DMS support, the way to ensure reliable transmission of multicast IPv6 RAs would be to sent them as Ethernet unicast over 802.11 media. This document is to express IETF interest to see 802.11 access points to sent IPv6 RAs with IPv6 destination address of ff02::1 (and the Ethernet destination address of 33:33:00:00:00:01) as Ethernet unicast packets to then connected clients.
